To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a lipidomic analysis was used to quantify changes in hepatic lipids over a 52-week period in a diet-induced murine model of nonalcohoic steatohepatits.

the progression of NAFLD is associated with changes in the lipidome that include increases in monounsaturated DAG and cholesterol esters, phosphatidic acids, phosphatidylethanoline, and lysolecithins.
the progression of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is associated with a decrease in phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylethanloamine, and phosphatidylserines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of lipid species that are associated with the progression of NAFLD to NASH and cirrhosis.
the development of a novel, non-invasive, optical technique to monitor the progression of liver fibrosis.
the development of novel therapies for the treatment of liver disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a lipidomic approach to nonalcoholic steatosis can provide a read out of disease progression.
a lipidomic readout of disease progression in a diet-induced mouse model of NAFLD revealed that multiple changes in lipid composition occur over time.

the progression of NAFLD to steatohepatosis is characterized by a decrease in the levels of phospholipids and plasmalogen phospholipids with a concomitant increase in diacylglycerol, ceramides, and globotrioseacylglycerol.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a high fat diet causes a rapid increase in monounsaturate containing DAG and cholesterol esters.
the progression of NAFLD is associated with changes in lipid species that are consistent with the development of insulin resistance, inflammation, fibrosis, and apoptosis.
the lipid changes associated with disease development are not necessarily the same as those associated with disease progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple lipid changes associated with disease.
lipid changes occur over time with disease progression and that the changes in lipid composition may be a readout of disease progression.
lipid species associated with disease progression are not the same as those that change with diet alone.
